title: Message Queue / Event Streaming: Kafka vs RabbitMQ vs SQS: when to use each, at-least-once vs exactly-once delivery, consumer groups, dead letter queues.
shortTitle: Message Queue / Event Streaming: Kafka vs RabbitMQ vs SQS
topicTitle: Messaging: Kafka vs RabbitMQ vs SQS
keyPoints: A message queue decouples producers from consumers, enabling asynchronous processing, buffering, and independent scaling.
RabbitMQ is a traditional broker with exchanges, rich routing, and per-message acknowledgement for moderate throughput.
Amazon SQS is a fully managed queue with at-least-once delivery and almost zero operational burden.
Apache Kafka is a distributed commit log for high-throughput streaming with replay and multiple consumer groups.
At-least-once delivery means consumers must be idempotent; exactly-once within Kafka uses transactional producers.
Consumer groups share partitions for parallelism; each message is processed once per group.
Dead-letter queues capture poison messages after a retry limit so they do not block the main queue.

s1_definition.oneliner: Decouple producers from consumers with a queue; pick RabbitMQ for routing, SQS for simple managed queues, Kafka for high-throughput replayable streams, and always plan delivery semantics and dead-letter handling.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Message queue** : an intermediary that decouples producers from consumers by passing messages asynchronously, enabling buffering, independent scaling, and resilience.
- **RabbitMQ** : a traditional message broker with exchanges, queues, and per-message acknowledgement, optimized for flexible routing and moderate throughput.
- **Amazon SQS** : a fully managed queue with at-least-once delivery (standard) or exactly-once (FIFO), requiring almost no operational burden.
- **Apache Kafka** : a distributed, partitioned, durable commit log optimized for high-throughput event streaming, replay, and multiple independent consumer groups.
- **Dead-letter queue (DLQ)** : a side queue that captures messages that fail processing after a retry limit, preventing a single poison message from blocking the main queue.
s1_definition.analogy: When Rajesh transfers money at National Bank of India, several things must follow: update the ledger, send a receipt, notify fraud monitoring. Instead of the transfer desk doing all of that while Rajesh waits, it drops a note in an internal mail system and moves on; other departments pick up their copies and act. That internal mail system is a message queue. RabbitMQ is like a smart mailroom that routes each letter to the right desk. SQS is a simple, reliable outbox managed by Amazon. Kafka is a permanent logbook many departments can read and re-read at their own pace.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A message queue or event streaming platform decouples producers from consumers through an intermediary, which enables asynchronous processing, buffering, and independent scaling. I always compare the three common choices by matching their guarantees to the problem. RabbitMQ is a traditional broker with exchanges and per-message acknowledgement, excellent when I need rich routing and moderate throughput. Amazon SQS is a fully managed queue that gives reliable at-least-once delivery with almost no operational burden, ideal when I just want a simple, dependable queue. Apache Kafka is a distributed, partitioned, durable log that retains messages for replay, which is the right choice for high-throughput event streaming, analytics pipelines, and letting many independent consumer groups read the same stream.

In the banking context at National Bank of India, this decoupling solved a real problem. The transfer service used to synchronously update the ledger, send a receipt, and notify fraud monitoring, so a slow email server slowed down every transfer. After publishing a transfer event to a topic and letting separate consumer groups handle the ledger, receipts, and fraud independently, the transfer returned immediately and each side effect proceeded at its own pace.

Two guarantees dominate my design thinking. The first is delivery semantics. At-least-once means a message can be redelivered, so I make consumers idempotent by recording a message id and skipping duplicates, which is simpler and more robust than chasing true exactly-once. The second is consumer groups: a group shares a topic's partitions among its members so each message is processed once per group, and I scale parallelism by adding members up to the partition count.

The operational details I never skip are dead-letter queues and ordering. A dead-letter queue captures messages that repeatedly fail after a retry limit, so a single poison message does not jam the queue or vanish silently, and I can investigate it later. Ordering is guaranteed only per partition, so when I need strict ordering for a particular account I partition by account id. Choosing the platform by matching its delivery, ordering, and retention guarantees to the domain is what makes an asynchronous banking system both fast and correct.

Remember one sentence: decouple with a queue, design idempotent consumers for at-least-once delivery, and use dead-letter queues so poison messages never block the pipeline.
